Q: Change node version using NVM and Docker-Compose A:
  1. Set the default node version as well (inside the shell script). I don't know why it's necessary but it works. So entrypoint.sh looks like this: 
    #!/bin/bash
source root/.nvm/nvm.sh && nvm use "$@" && nvm alias default "$@"
node --version
exec /usr/sbin/init
  2. When running Bash with docker exec -it <container_id> /bin/sh -c "node --version" and not in interactive mode or login to shell it will not read startup scripts so node version set by using source /root/.nvm/nvm.sh and nvm use XXX is not red and that's why it's not changed for this Bash session. Solution is to login to container and run node --version from within or source nvm.sh as well before running node --version e.g.: docker exec -it <container_id> sh -c "source /root/.nvm/nvm.sh && node --version".

Q: With Excel VBA, creating a ZIP folder with all files in a specific folder A:

Here's a basic example using VBA:

Sub Tester()

    Dim colFiles As New Collection
    colFiles.Add "C:\Temp\Timer.log"
    colFiles.Add "C:\Temp\Sig.html"
    colFiles.Add "C:\Temp\file listing.txt"
    
    CreateZip "C:\Temp\Test.zip", colFiles
End Sub

'Create a zip file at `zipFullPath` and add the files specified
'   in `filesToAdd`
Sub CreateZip(zipFullPath As String, filesToAdd As Collection)
    Dim el
    ' `NewZip` from https://jkp-ads.com/rdb/win/s7/win001.htm
    If Len(Dir(zipFullPath)) > 0 Then Kill zipFullPath
    Open zipFullPath For Output As #1
    Print #1, Chr$(80) & Chr$(75) & Chr$(5) & Chr$(6) & String(18, 0)
    Close #1
    
    With CreateObject("Shell.Application")
        For Each el In filesToAdd  'loop files to add
            'Shell prefers Variant to String...
            .Namespace(CVar(zipFullPath)).copyhere el
        Next
    End With
End Sub

Q: Langgraph Studio Multi-Agent Example: Hierarchical Agents? A:

The key to hierarchical multi-agent systems in LangGraph is using **subgraphs** — each agent is its own StateGraph` that gets composed into a parent supervisor graph. Here is a working pattern:

1. Define Individual Agent Subgraphs

from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, MessagesState, START, END
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o")

# Research Agent subgraph
def research_agent(state: MessagesState):
    response = llm.invoke([
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a research agent. Find information."},
        *state["messages"]
    ])
    return {"messages": [response]}

research_graph = StateGraph(MessagesState)
research_graph.add_node("research", research_agent)
research_graph.add_edge(START, "research")
research_graph.add_edge("research", END)
research_subgraph = research_graph.compile()

# Writer Agent subgraph  
def writer_agent(state: MessagesState):
    response = llm.invoke([
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a writing agent. Draft content."},
        *state["messages"]
    ])
    return {"messages": [response]}

writer_graph = StateGraph(MessagesState)
writer_graph.add_node("writer", writer_agent)
writer_graph.add_edge(START, "writer")
writer_graph.add_edge("writer", END)
writer_subgraph = writer_graph.compile()

2. Build the Supervisor (Parent Graph)

from typing import Literal

def supervisor(state: MessagesState) -> dict:
    response = llm.invoke([
        {"role": "system", "content": """You are a supervisor managing agents: 
        'researcher' and 'writer'. Route tasks to the right agent.
        Respond with JSON: {"next": "researcher"|"writer"|"FINISH"}"""},
        *state["messages"]
    ])
    # Parse routing decision
    content = response.content
    if "researcher" in content.lower():
        return {"next": "researcher"}
    elif "writer" in content.lower():
        return {"next": "writer"}
    return {"next": "FINISH"}

def route_supervisor(state) -> Literal["researcher", "writer", "__end__"]:
    return state.get("next", "__end__")

# Parent graph with subgraphs as nodes
parent = StateGraph(MessagesState)
parent.add_node("supervisor", supervisor)
parent.add_node("researcher", research_subgraph)  # subgraph as node
parent.add_node("writer", writer_subgraph)         # subgraph as node

parent.add_edge(START, "supervisor")
parent.add_conditional_edges("supervisor", route_supervisor)
parent.add_edge("researcher", "supervisor")  # return to supervisor
parent.add_edge("writer", "supervisor")      # return to supervisor

graph = parent.compile()

3. LangGraph Studio Compatibility

For Studio, save this as graph.py and create a langgraph.json:

{
  "graphs": {
    "agent": "./graph.py:graph"
  },
  "env": ".env"
}

Key Points

  • Subgraphs are the mechanism for hierarchy — each compiled StateGraph can be a node in a parent graph
  • The supervisor pattern routes messages to child agents and they return control back
  • State flows through MessagesState so all agents share conversation context
  • For deeper hierarchies, a child agent can itself be a supervisor with its own subgraphs
  • Use add_conditional_edges for the routing logic from the supervisor

This pattern works natively in LangGraph Studio since it just needs the compiled top-level graph. The Studio will visualize the full hierarchy including subgraph internals.`

Q: Casting functions with pointer arguments to function pointers with void* argument A:

C23 §6.2.5(33) guarantees,

A pointer to void shall have the same representation and alignment requirements as a pointer to a character type. Similarly, pointers to qualified or unqualified versions of compatible types shall have the same representation and alignment requirements. All pointers to structure types shall have the same representation and alignment requirements as each other. All pointers to union types shall have the same representation and alignment requirements as each other. Pointers to other types may not have the same representation or alignment requirements

Where “a pointer to a character type” means char*, unsigned char* or signed char*. (Same section, paragraph 20.) Therefore, if the only difference in the signature is changing a pointer parameter from between these four types, with or without const/volatile qualifiers, the pointers must have the same representation and it will work. Passing the function any other type of pointer (including int*) might not. Two different structure or union types are not formally pointer-interconvertible, so passing a pointer to one structure type as a pointer to another structure type will get a pointer with the correct format, but which might not be valid.

The historical reason for this is that C89 added the void* type and wanted functions that took void* to be callable from K&R-style code. One important use case was that it changed the specification of several standard-library functions like memcpy() to take void* instead of char*. They required void* and char* to have the same representation so that code that declared memcpy() the classic K&R way, and code that used the new ANSI prototype, could both link to the same implementation and work.

For other pointer types, that code will definitely break on any of the real-world implementations that have different encodings of word pointers and byte pointers. I could also imagine a memory-sanitizing implementation checking that the value being passed in is a valid pointer of the correct type and flagging this as a runtime error. You might therefore want to code defensively even on compilers where casting the function pointer works.
